Claude,2026-08-21T21:09:31.097734Z,"This is exactly the closing anchor I needed: the Punta Carnero maize date of **4857 cal BC** falls almost precisely at my atlas end-point (4,500 BC) and documents the ""Vegas–Valdivia hiatus"" — a genuinely important, citable transitional data point. I now have a comprehensive, well-sourced framework. Let me compile everything into the deliverable.
# Step 1 Deliverable: Scientific & Chronological Framework, 13,000–4,500 BC
### Ecuador and the adjacent southern Colombia / northern Peru / Pacific littoral study region
## A. Chronological Table

I divided the 8,500-year span into **four phases**, based on documented environmental and archaeological transitions rather than equal time blocks. Boundaries are approximate and some sources disagree by centuries — this is flagged in the Confidence column.
| Phase | BC dates (cal) | cal BP equivalent | Environment | Archaeological evidence | Confidence |

| **1. Late Glacial / Terminal Pleistocene** | ~13,000–10,900 BC | ~14,950–12,850 cal BP | Andes still hold expanded glaciers retreating from Local Last Glacial Maximum positions; equatorial glacier margins at times reached as low as ~3,000 m in the eastern Andes of Colombia/Ecuador/N. Peru during the LGM, most Andean glaciers moved down slope and reached their lowermost positions at about 3000 m in the eastern Andes of Colombia, Ecuador and northern Peru. Andean highlands largely treeless páramo/steppe; Amazon-facing slopes cooler than today. Global sea level still tens of meters below present, rising through Meltwater Pulse 1A (~14,700–13,500 BP) Meltwater pulse 1A is the name used for a period of rapid post-glacial sea level rise between 14,700 and 13,500 years ago, during which global sea level rose between 16 and 25 meters in about 400–500 years. | Earliest secure regional evidence dates to the very end of this phase. Highland Ecuador's Cubilán site (Cu–27) has two radiocarbon dates ranging between ~12,550 and 11,770 cal BP, described as the second oldest archaeological site so far registered for Ecuador. Megafauna (gomphotheres, giant ground sloths) present and regionally hunted elsewhere in South America, but **no confirmed human–megafauna kill association yet documented on the Santa Elena Peninsula** there is no evidence of interaction between Late Pleistocene humans and extinct megafauna on the Santa Elena Peninsula, despite substantial archaeological research in the area. Tanque Loma megafaunal bone bed (~17,000–23,500 rcyBP) predates this phase and has no confirmed artifact association. | **B–C.** Sparse, low-density record; chronology described by specialists as having ""hygiene problems"" chronological hygiene problems have been noted in sites like Chobshi, El Inga, and San José, such as the lack of correspondence between dates and recovered lithic types and the lack of association between radiocarbon or obsidian hydration samples and registered stratigraphic units or artifact typology. |

| **2. Pleistocene–Holocene Transition (incl. Younger Dryas)** | ~10,900–9,650 BC | ~12,850–11,600 cal BP | Younger Dryas cold/dry reversal affects the northern tropics; regional signal is spatially complex — a southward shift in the ITCZ at the start of the YD could explain colder conditions in the northern tropics while precipitation-sensitive glaciers advanced in the southern tropical mountains, with a northerly shift after ~12,650 cal BP explaining increased moisture-balance and warming in the northern Andes. A high-resolution local record from Laguna Llaviucu (Ecuador Andes) documents ~4 °C warming during the glacial termination beginning ~16,800 years ago, with stable temperatures in the early-to-mid Holocene. Sea level still well below present but rising fast; Santa Elena coastal plain substantially wider than today. Megafauna under increasing stress. | **This is the richest early-occupation phase.** El Inga (highland, near Quito): AMS-dated fishtail-point occupation, with the type site described as the earliest documented evidence of inhabitants of the Quito plateau, a Paleoindian site (12,500–9,000 cal BP). Cubilán area continues. ""Pre-Las Vegas"" coastal occupation begins by ~10,800 BP it is clear that people were living in the highlands and along the southwest Ecuadorian littoral between 11,000 and 10,000 BP. Sangolquí (interandean valley, Pichincha) sites dated 13,500–4,500 BP span from this phase through Phase 4. In Colombia, highland Sabana de Bogotá sites (Tequendama etc.) show occupation from 13,525 cal BP. In Peru, earliest Paiján/unifacial coastal sites from 11,650 BP at El Palto in the upper Zaña Valley, with Amotape- and Talara-like sites possibly as early as 11,000 BP. | **B for El Inga's broad dating; A for its existence.** Site-specific chronologies (El Inga, Chobshi, San José) are individually contested even where the general presence of people in this window is not. |

| **3. Early Holocene** | ~9,650–6,600 BC | ~11,600–8,550 cal BP | Warming and moistening trend continues; páramo vegetation widely dominated the landscape during the LGM/Late Glacial with the upper forest line at least ~700 m lower in the northern part of the study transect, then rises through the Early Holocene. Polylepis forest widespread Polylepis was widespread during the warm early Holocene. Coastal Santa Elena: initially arid littoral with seasonal estuaries and mangrove episodes. Global sea level rise continues, slowing after ~8,000–7,000 BP as it approaches near-modern levels. Megafauna collapse underway: the megafauna definitively abandoned the Cordillera areas around 12,000 yr BP due to increasing aridity, and subsequently migrated to coastal areas such as the Santa Elena Peninsula and Amazonian areas. | **Las Vegas culture, Santa Elena Peninsula** — the best-documented adaptation in the study area. Early Las Vegas (10,000 to 8,000 BP) and Late Las Vegas (8,000 to 6,600 BP) phases are described from artifacts, burials, settlement data, faunal remains, pollen, and phytoliths; people were unspecialized hunters, fishermen, and gatherers who added plant cultivation to their subsistence system before 8,000 years ago, with Cucurbita phytoliths directly dated to 10,130–9,320 ¹⁴C years BP identified as domesticated based on size, following earlier exploitation of a wild Cucurbita species in the terminal Pleistocene. In N. Peru, Paiján and the Nanchoc tradition (unifacial, plant-processing focus) develop in the Zaña/Jequetepeque valleys; coca chewing is directly dated to at least 8,000 cal BP at Nanchoc. Megafaunal-artifact association claimed at El Cautivo, Santa Elena, though sample size is small since only a few tools have yet been identified at El Cautivo, an accurate comparison with the Las Vegas lithic assemblages is not possible; however, El Cautivo contains the oldest artifacts and tools associated with megafauna in Ecuador. | **A** for Las Vegas overall chronology (30 dates, internally consistent); **B** for specific behavioral interpretations (cultivation intensity, sedentism level); **C** for El Cautivo human–megafauna association given small sample. |

| **4. Middle Holocene (to 4,500 BC)** | ~6,600–4,500 BC | ~8,550–6,450 cal BP | Vegetation and coastal systems approach a more modern configuration; sea level nears present position — mid-Holocene stabilization is directly dated on the Ecuadorian coast: records document mid-Holocene sea-level stabilization, development of low-energy depositional environments, and variation in rainfall attributable to ENSO by 5,000 cal BC. Upper montane forest and reduced páramo extent through much of the Holocene thermal optimum, before later Holocene shifts. Interandean valleys periodically reshaped by major volcanic/lahar events from Cotopaxi and other centers. | **Late Las Vegas phase ends by ~4,600 BC**, followed by a documented gap before ceramic Valdivia (~3,500 BC): archaeologists found no more evidence of the culture after 4,600 BC; it was one thousand years later, around 3,500 BC, that Valdivia culture appears. Critically, this ""hiatus"" is now partly filled: the Punta Carnero core provided the first evidence for occupation of the peninsula during the hiatus between Vegas and Valdivia, with maize present in a stratum dating to 4,857 cal BC — almost exactly the atlas's closing date. Highland interandean occupation continues at Sangolquí through this phase, with Cotopaxi lahar activity reshaping the landscape around 4,500 BP (note: this is a BP, not BC, figure — see chronology caution below). In Peru, Nanchoc plant-management intensifies toward incipient horticulture. | **A** for the Vegas end-date and Punta Carnero maize date (both directly dated); **B** for interpreting this as genuine demographic/cultural discontinuity versus a survey/preservation gap. |

**Important chronology caution for the atlas:** The Sangolquí paper's ""4,500 BP"" lahar-reshaping date is expressed in **uncalibrated/conventional BP**, not BC — do not silently convert this to ""4,500 BC."" At face value, 4,500 BP calibrates to roughly 3,300–3,000 cal BC, which is **after** the atlas's end date. I flag this now so it is not miscoded later; the Sangolquí early-occupation window (13,500–4,500 BP) itself spans roughly 11,500 BC to ~3,000 BC in calibrated terms, meaning only its earlier portion falls inside 13,000–4,500 BC.
## B. Major scientific questions the map should communicate

1. **How does the human presence relate to deglaciation and rising sea level?** — did people occupy the coast only after (or during) the exposure/drowning of the shelf, and how much land was lost to MWP-1A and subsequent Holocene rise?

2. **Was there a highland-first or coast-first colonization of what is now Ecuador?** — El Inga (highland) and ""Pre-Vegas"" coastal sites are broadly contemporary but each individually has dating uncertainty; the map should show this as an open question, not a resolved sequence.

3. **What was the relationship between humans and megafauna?** — the evidence supports temporal overlap and possibly indirect ecological pressure (habitat compression into refugia like Santa Elena) but not a confirmed hunting/kill-site pattern in Ecuador specifically.

4. **How did the Younger Dryas affect human settlement patterns, if at all?** — regional paleoclimate shows a complex, non-uniform signal (drier in some records, wetter in others depending on ITCZ position); the archaeological record in this window is thin enough that human response cannot be confidently reconstructed.

5. **When and how did plant cultivation begin, and is it locally developed or introduced?** — Las Vegas Cucurbita evidence is among the earliest in the Americas; the map should communicate this as a regionally significant, well-evidenced developmental trajectory.

6. **What connected the highlands, the coast, and the region beyond modern Ecuador?** — obsidian, and later maize/coca corridors, imply interaction networks, but the well-dated long-distance obsidian trade (Mullumica) is mostly a **later** (Formative-period, post-3,000 BC) phenomenon — the map must not backdate it into the Paleoindian period without qualification.

7. **What happened between Las Vegas and Valdivia?** — the ~1,000-year ""hiatus"" is a real, citable archaeological question, now partially addressed by the 4,857 cal BC Punta Carnero maize find, which anchors the atlas's closing chronology.

8. **How much of the ""Ecuadorian"" archaeological pattern is actually a wider northern Andean / north-Peruvian coastal pattern?** — Paiján, Nanchoc, and Sabana de Bogotá evidence show broadly parallel (not identical) trajectories, justifying the cross-border study area on scientific rather than political grounds.
## C. Datasets / evidence categories required for the final map
| Category | Status | Key sources identified |
| Topography (modern DEM base) | Standard GIS base layer — no scientific sourcing issue | (to be sourced at production stage) |

| Geology relevant to occupation | Volcanic stratigraphy (Cotopaxi, Antisana, Galeras), obsidian source geology (Mullumica, Yanaurco-Quiscatola, Cordillera Real domes) | Hall & Mothes (Cotopaxi eruptive history); Barberi et al. (Antisana); Burger, Asaro et al. 1994; Knight et al. 2010 |

| Paleocoastline / sea level | Global eustatic curve (Fairbanks/Barbados) + local tectonic-uplift-adjusted modeling specific to Santa Elena | Fairbanks 1989 (Nature); Stothert et al. 2003 (Quaternary International) — includes an explicit paleocoastline reconstruction using isobaths and uplift-rate modeling |

| Glaciers | Regional glacial chronology (moraine mapping, cosmogenic/¹⁴C dating) — data exists but authors explicitly note dating is sparse | Rodbell, Smith & Mark 2009; Clapperton 1993; Heine & Heine 1996; Jomelli et al. (Younger Dryas glacier advances) |
| Hydrology | Major river systems tied to Cotopaxi lahar pathways and coastal drainages (Guayas, Zaña, Jequetepeque valleys) | Mothes, Hall & Janda 1998 (Chillos Valley Lahar) |

| Vegetation / land cover | Strong pollen-core network across Ecuadorian Andes and one high-resolution long record (Llaviucu) | Colinvaux et al. 1988, 1997; Hansen et al. 2003; Bakker et al. 2008; **Chen/Rodbell et al. 2024 (Llaviucu, PNAS)** |

| Archaeological sites | Point data exists for a defined, citable set: El Inga, Cubilán (Cu-27, Cu-26), San José, Montequinto, Las Vegas complex (32 sites, 9 dated), El Cautivo, Sangolquí sites, Tequendama/Aguazuque (Colombia), Paiján/Nanchoc sites (Peru) | Pagán-Jiménez et al. 2021 (Cubilán dataset); Stothert et al. 2003; Dillehay et al.; Correal 1989 |

| Raw material sources | Obsidian sourcing is well studied but mostly documents later (Formative) exploitation intensity, not confirmed Paleoindian-period sourcing | Burger, Asaro, Michel, Stross & Salazar 1994; Knight et al. 2010 |

| Mobility/interaction corridors | Kelp Highway hypothesis is a Pacific-wide framework but explicitly **breaks down in the tropics** (mangrove/reef replace kelp) — direct application to Ecuador's coast is Category C hypothesis, not documented local evidence | Erlandson et al. 2007; Frontiers 2025 (kelp poleward-shift review) |
